title: Adding a second brood box
subtitle: Giving a strong spring colony room to grow before it swarms.
excerpt: A colony that has packed the bottom brood box with brood and bees by late April needs more space or it will swarm. Adding a second national box above the first gives the queen room to lay and the workers room to store nectar. Here is the inspection sequence that tells you it is time, and the steps for fitting the second box.
sourceNotes: British Beekeepers Association, Swarm Management (BBKA information sheet). NBU Beekeeper's Toolkit (2024), section on spring management and colony expansion. Frank Pearson, Bee-keeping for All (1923), chapters on spring colony management, Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: The lower box of a hive where the queen lays eggs and brood is raised. Also called the brood chamber. Separate from the supers above the queen excluder.
The area within the brood chamber where the queen is actively laying and sealed brood, larvae, and eggs are present.
A band of freshly collected nectar stored above and around the brood nest on the upper frames. A sign that the bees are bringing in a nectar flow and that the hive is congested.

content.text: A national hive on a single
brood box
fills quickly in a good spring. Once seven or eight frames carry brood, the colony starts thinking about swarming. A second brood box gives the queen room to expand the
brood nest
downward and buys several more weeks before congestion triggers swarm preparations.
Signs the colony needs more room
Seven or more brood frames, most covered solidly in sealed brood.
A
nectar arch
on the top third of most frames, reducing the space the queen has to lay.
A heavy cluster of bees hanging below the bottom of the frames on warm evenings (bearding).
Any queen cells begun on the face of frames or at the bottom of combs.
How to fit the second box
Open the hive and inspect all frames. Remove any queen cells you find. Confirm the queen is present and laying.

Take three or four frames of sealed brood from the centre of the existing brood box and move them into the new second box. The second box can sit below the existing one (nadiring) or above it. Most UK beekeepers nadir: placing the new box underneath the colony so the queen moves down into fresh comb.
Fill the spaces left in the existing box with new, drawn comb or foundation frames. Place these in the centre where the brood frames were.
Add drawn or foundation frames to the new second box to fill all eleven spaces. Empty frames placed around the moved brood frames.
If using the double-brood method, remove the queen excluder. Let the queen move freely between both boxes.
Reassemble the hive: floor, lower brood box, upper brood box, queen excluder, supers if any, crown board, roof. Check all boxes are aligned and the entrance is clear.
What to check a week later

A week after adding the second box, open and check that the queen has begun laying in the new box. You should see eggs and young larvae in the new frames. If not, check that she has not been blocked by a queen excluder accidentally left between the two boxes.

attrs.cue: Queen nowhere to be found after the reorganisation
attrs.cause: She may have slipped into the new box during the frame transfer and is now laying there
attrs.fix: Check both boxes thoroughly. Look for eggs in both upper and lower frames before assuming queenlessness.

attrs.cue: Colony still raising queen cells a week later
attrs.cause: The colony is already in swarm preparation and the extra space has not relieved the impulse
attrs.fix: Remove all open and sealed queen cells except one good sealed cell. Consider an artificial swarm or split.
